posts.title: Why we keep the room open at 15:00
posts.excerpt: A quiet look at why Kohaku Brasserie keeps its doors open through the afternoon quiet hours, offering an unhurried table for coffee, warm plates, and contemplation.
posts.content:
At three in the afternoon, most restaurant dining rooms across the city fall dark. Shutters are lowered, front doors are locked from within, and staff hurry away into the streets until the evening rush begins. When Inès Marchetti and Tomasz Lindqvist founded Kohaku Brasserie in 2014 at 14 Arcade Row in the Old Exchange Quarter, they chose a different path. They believed that a genuine brasserie belongs to the continuous fabric of its neighborhood. Locking the doors at 14:30 felt like turning away friends who simply needed a peaceful corner to pause, reflect, or converse.

The quiet hours between 14:30 and 18:00 possess an atmosphere found at no other point in our service day. As the brisk energy of lunch subsides, the room transforms. Crisp white linen is lifted from several tables to reveal the warmth of bare timber. The daylight changes its angle, slanting low through our tall windows to cast long shadows across the cobblestones of Arcade Row outside. The room becomes calm, spacious, and meditative. In the kitchen, the morning rush is cleared, and the evening prep begins without haste under the watchful eye of Tomasz Lindqvist.

During these hours, food is simple and grounding. We offer our afternoon plate for €16, bringing together warm crusty bread, cultured butter, braised seasonal beans, and mature cheese on dark stoneware. Pastry chef Kenji Albrecht-Mori brings fresh afternoon tarts from the ovens, filling the dining hall with comforting aromas of baked fruit and warm crust. Guests drop in without booking for parties of four or fewer, ordering a freshly brewed coffee or a quiet glass of wine poured by Lucía Ferreira from our selection of wines by the glass starting from €7.

There is an unmistakable hospitality in keeping a table open when others are shuttered. We often see solitary visitors sitting by the window with an open notebook, or colleagues meeting over coffee to discuss ideas away from formal offices. One of our favorite memories at Kohaku Brasserie began precisely at this hour: a 15:00 coffee meeting that ran smoothly into the late sitting. As afternoon turned into dusk, the coffee cups gave way to evening plates and wine, and the conversation stretched across six hours without anyone feeling rushed or unwelcome.

At 18:00, the tempo gently rises once more. Inès Marchetti and our floor staff reset the room for dinner, lighting the warm tungsten lamps and welcoming evening arrivals. But the quiet hours leave their mark on the room, anchoring its character as an unhurried sanctuary rather than a hurried commercial machine. Later, when Daniel Okafor steps onto the floor for the late sitting from 22:00 to midnight, that same unhurried spirit remains intact. Keeping our room open at 15:00 is not merely about serving an afternoon plate; it is our way of keeping faith with the true purpose of a city brasserie.

posts.title: Autumn on the pass
posts.excerpt: What changes on the pass when the nights draw in: brown butter, roasted fish and a heavier hand with the lamps.
posts.content:
The first cold week changes the pass before it changes the menu. Tomasz Lindqvist moves the heat lamps lower, the plates come out darker and warmer, and the brown butter gets a little more time in the pan.

This month the dinner à la carte carries a roast fish with brown butter and thyme, served on dark stoneware so the sauce looks like what it is. Mains start at €24, and the counter menu at the pass, six courses for €78, follows the same plates in smaller portions.

Lucía Ferreira has matched the fish with two whites and a light red from the glass list. Ask at the bar; she will pour a taste before you decide.

posts.title: The late sitting playlist
posts.excerpt: Low volume, long tracks: how the room sounds after 22:00, and why the playlist changes every Monday.
posts.content:
At 22:00 the late sitting begins and the room changes its voice. The lamps drop, the candles go on the tables, and the music turns from lunchtime brightness to something slower and quieter.

Daniel Okafor keeps the playlist: long tracks, few words, nothing that asks to be listened to. It is set once a week and shared in the Monday letter, so regulars can hear what is coming before they book.

The late-sitting menu is three courses for €52. The kitchen takes last orders at 23:15, and the room closes at midnight.
